profile.reading:
Switch: The Rock sits on Switch's Round Rock, Texas campus, at Dell Technologies' global headquarters address in Williamson County, part of the Austin metro. Switch announced the Texas campus, its fifth "PRIME" development, on June 2, 2021, naming it "The Rock" and simultaneously agreeing to acquire Data Foundry, a two-decades-established Austin and Houston colocation operator, contributing more than 500,000 square feet and 60 megawatts of existing capacity to the combined Texas footprint. Switch's own materials state The Rock campus alone offers more than 1.5 million square feet of data center space, with the full Texas ecosystem, Rock plus the acquired Data Foundry sites, exceeding 2 million square feet and a stated 185 megawatts of total capacity at the time of the 2021 announcement. Switch does not publish this site's exact street address, campus acreage, or a confirmed opening date; the popular association of "The Rock" name with a former limestone quarry does not appear anywhere in Switch's own published materials and is not confirmed here. An August 2026 Switch statement responding to Texas Governor Greg Abbott's data center standards discloses that Switch has committed more than $250 million in local investment under a long-term economic development agreement with the City of Round Rock generating tax revenue through 2037, and pledges cooperation with ERCOT, the Public Utility Commission of Texas, and local communities on noise mitigation, lighting controls, setbacks, and traffic improvements. Switch markets the campus under its self-created "Tier 5" branding rather than an Uptime Institute Tier certification, and states 100 percent renewable energy sourced through renewable energy credit purchases rather than direct on-site generation.

Round Rock and the broader Williamson County area have drawn substantial technology-sector investment beyond Switch, including major semiconductor manufacturing nearby, part of a broader Central Texas corridor stretching from Austin through Georgetown and Taylor that has become one of the fastest-growing U.S. technology and advanced-manufacturing regions over the past decade. Switch's Data Foundry acquisition, folded into the Rock campus's combined Texas capacity figures, gave Switch an immediate operating presence in both Austin and Houston rather than requiring it to build out Texas capacity entirely from scratch.

reading.body:
Switch: The Rock is a 1.5 million square foot data center campus under development at Dell Technologies' global headquarters in Round Rock, with a stated planned IT capacity of 185 megawatts. At a typical AI training density of 40 kilowatts per rack, 185 MW translates to approximately 4,600 racks. The campus operates under Switch's proprietary "Tier 5" branding rather than third-party certification and sources 100 percent renewable energy through renewable energy credits rather than on-site generation. Switch has committed more than $250 million in local investment under an agreement with Round Rock extending through 2037, pledging coordination with ERCOT and the Texas Public Utility Commission on grid integration, noise mitigation, and infrastructure impacts.

The Rock anchors Switch's broader Texas footprint, which includes more than 500,000 square feet of acquired colocation capacity from Data Foundry spanning Austin and Houston, bringing the combined Texas ecosystem to more than 2 million square feet and 185 megawatts of total stated capacity as of 2021. The region already hosts substantial semiconductor manufacturing and has emerged as one of the fastest-growing U.S. technology and advanced manufacturing corridors, with major investment concentrated in a Central Texas stretch from Austin through Georgetown and Taylor. Switch's acquisition of Data Foundry gave the operator an immediate operating presence in two major metropolitan areas rather than requiring build-out from bare land.

At 185 megawatts of published capacity, The Rock ranks 19th among all facilities in Texas, below the state's published total of 468 megawatts across 18 facilities with disclosed figures. Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities in total, the vast majority of which publish no capacity number. The Rock's position reflects both its substantial scale within Texas and the limited visibility into actual capacity across the state's broader data center footprint, which includes older colocation, cloud regional nodes, and undisclosed enterprise infrastructure alongside newer AI-focused builds.
